Clerical
klĕr´ĭ-kal
adj. (pertaining to the clergy; belonging to the ordained ministry as a distinct order)
Greek kleros, a lot or inheritance — and here is the irony that governs the whole entry: 1 Peter 5:3 uses kleros of the flock, warning elders not to be lords over God's heritage. The word that became “clergy” is the Bible's word for the laity.

Biblical Definition

Clerical describes the ordained as a class. The New Testament's word-history runs the other way: elders are told to feed the flock, “neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock” (1Pe 5:3) — and heritage there is kleros, the root of clergy, used of the congregation. Office exists to equip, not to replace: Christ gave pastors and teachers “for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ” (Eph 4:11–12). Gifts are distributed to all: “the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal” (1Co 12:7). The whole church is a priesthood (1Pe 2:9). And the apostles kept to their own work: “we will give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word” (Act 6:4).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines clerical as relating to the clergy, or to a clerk; and clergy as the body of men set apart, by due ordination, to the service of God in the Christian church.

expand to see more

CLERICAL, a. Relating or pertaining to the clergy; as clerical tonsure; clerical robes; clerical duties.

CLERGY, n. The body of men set apart, by due ordination, to the service of God, in the christian church.

The word is derived from the Greek word signifying a lot, inheritance or portion.

Key Scripture

1Pe 5:3 — "Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock."

Eph 4:11 — "And he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers;"

Eph 4:12 — "For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ:"

1Co 12:7 — "But the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal."

Act 6:4 — "But we will give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word."

Modern Corruption

The ministry becomes a caste, and Ephesians 4 gives it as an equipping office for a working church.

expand to see more

Webster's own entry preserves the point without pressing it: the word comes from the Greek for a lot or inheritance. In 1 Peter 5:3 that word names the flock — God's heritage, His allotted portion — and the elders are warned not to lord it over them. Somewhere between the apostle and the Middle Ages the term migrated from the people to the officers, and the migration was not a mere accident of vocabulary; it marked a church in which the ordained had become the church and the rest had become its audience.

Ephesians 4:11–12 gives the corrective and its punctuation matters. Christ gave apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body. Read straight, the officers equip the saints, and the saints do the work of the ministry. That single clause reorganises a congregation: the pastor is not the man who does the church's work while others watch, but the man whose work is to make the others able. The chapter's endpoint is a body in which every joint supplieth and every part works in measure.

None of this abolishes the office, and the anticlerical reading of these verses is its own error. Acts 6 exists precisely because the apostles refused to be diverted from prayer and the ministry of the word — they created an office rather than diluting theirs. First Timothy says elders who rule well are worthy of double honour, and Hebrews tells a congregation to obey them that have the rule over them. The Reformed position is neither a priestly caste nor a church with no officers, but ordained men who are inside the brotherhood and accountable within it, doing a distinct work for a congregation that has work of its own.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek kleros (G2819), a lot, inheritance, heritage; katartismos (G2677), perfecting, equipping; diakonia (G1248), ministry, service; phanerosis (G5321), manifestation.

expand to see more

Greek kleros (G2819) — lot, heritage; 1 Peter 5:3 — of the flock; also Acts 1:26, Colossians 1:12.

Greek katartismos (G2677) — perfecting, equipping; Ephesians 4:12 only.

Greek diakonia (G1248) — ministry, service; Ephesians 4:12, Acts 6:4, 2 Corinthians 5:18.

Usage

"“Lords over God's heritage” — and heritage is the word that became clergy."

"“For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry” — read straight."

"“Given to every man to profit withal” — every man."
